The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(1,1)$ and lies on both $y=f(x)$ and $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)=$
{{field-1}}
worked_solution:
Since $A\,(1,1)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(1)=1.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(1)=-2.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
